Find and correct the restriction, such as undersized or crushed duct, a restrictive filter, or closed registers, then re-measure static and airflow
Seal the return grille partly so static pressure numbers come down

questions.explanation: High external static with low airflow is a duct or restriction problem, and charging over it hides the fault while leaving capacity, noise, and coil problems behind. Options A and B use refrigerant to mask an air-side defect, and option D restricts the return further and would raise, not lower, the blower burden.

questions.question: A stacked closet in a multifamily unit houses a water heater below and an air handler above, with barely enough room to remove the air handler's filter. Why is this arrangement a service concern worth documenting?

answers.text: Because stacked equipment voids the water heater warranty automatically, and documentation is needed only to assign warranty responsibility later
Because filters in stacked closets never need changing, so the concern is limited to the appearance of the installation in inspection photographs
Because water heaters in a shared closet heat the return air so much that cooling capacity is lost, and documentation triggers a larger cooling unit
Because inadequate access leads to skipped maintenance and unsafe workarounds, and filters, drains, and shutoffs must remain reachable for routine service

questions.explanation: Tight stacked closets cause real maintenance failures when filters, drains, and shutoffs cannot be reached, so access problems should be documented and corrected. The issue is not automatic warranty loss or appearance, and closet heat from a water heater is not the primary capacity concern.

questions.question: A homeowner who lives in a single-family house that is her principal residence wants to replace a failed component on her own furnace herself. A neighbor insists state trade licensure bars her from doing any of this work. Who is right?

answers.text: The homeowner may do the work, since the licensing chapter does not prohibit an owner from working on the owner's principal residence of this kind
The neighbor is right, because every repair to a fuel-burning appliance in any dwelling must be performed by a licensed master or a person working under one
The homeowner may do the work only after obtaining a specialty sublicense, which is the credential the state issues to owners for work on their own homes
The neighbor is right unless the home is farm property, because the owner exemption in the licensing chapter is limited strictly to agricultural buildings and land

questions.explanation: A is correct: the licensing chapter does not prohibit an owner from performing work on the owner's principal residence where it is an existing dwelling not larger than a single-family dwelling meeting the stated conditions. B is wrong because the owner provision is an express carve-out from the chapter's reach. C is wrong because no owner specialty sublicense is required for this exempt work. D is wrong because the provision covers a qualifying principal residence, not farm property alone.

questions.question: A dryer exhaust layout uses two 90-degree elbows and one 45-degree elbow. Taking the general maximum equivalent length of 35 feet, reduced by 5 feet for each 90-degree elbow and 2.5 feet for each 45-degree elbow, what is the longest actual straight duct run this layout may use?

answers.text: 22.5 feet of straight duct, with the three elbows consuming 12.5 feet of the length allowance the exhaust system is permitted overall
35.0 feet of straight duct, with elbow deductions applied only when the manufacturer's instructions for the dryer are unavailable to the installer
27.5 feet of straight duct, with each of the three elbows charged at the gentler 45-degree rate since the duct turns gradually at each fitting
47.5 feet of straight duct, with each elbow adding its deduction figure to the allowance in the same way a longer vent raises a chimney's capacity

questions.explanation: A is correct: deductions = (2 x 5 ft) + (1 x 2.5 ft) = 12.5 ft; permitted straight run = 35 ft - 12.5 ft = 22.5 ft. B is wrong because the fitting deductions apply to the general 35-foot maximum as part of the standard calculation. C is wrong because the two 90-degree elbows are charged at the 5-foot rate for their angle, not at the 45-degree rate. D is wrong because fittings consume allowance; they never add to it.

hawaii-c40-hvac.quiz_title: Hawaii C-40 HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: No-cool call on an R-410A system with verified normal airflow. Readings: suction 105 psig, head pressure near normal at 285 psig, suction superheat 26 degrees F, liquid subcooling 18 degrees F, and a 7-degree temperature drop measured across the liquid-line filter drier with light frost just downstream of it. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: Low refrigerant charge, which would starve the evaporator but also leave subcooling very low because little liquid backs up in the condenser, unlike the 18 degrees measured here
An overfeeding expansion valve, which would drive superheat down toward zero and flood the suction line rather than hold superheat at 26 degrees
Noncondensables in the system, which would push head pressure and subcooling up together and would not create a localized temperature drop and frost at one component
A restricted liquid-line filter drier

questions.explanation: High superheat with high subcooling means liquid is backing up behind a restriction while the evaporator starves, and the 7-degree drop with frost across the drier locates that restriction exactly. Low charge gives low subcooling, an overfeeding valve collapses superheat, and noncondensables raise head pressure without frosting one component in the liquid line.

questions.question: A homeowner asks why the new R-454B air handler runs its blower for a while after a leak sensor trips, even though cooling has stopped. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The blower is removing residual heat from the electric heat strips, a normal cool-down sequence that happens to coincide with the sensor alarm event
The blower pressurizes the duct system so refrigerant vapor is forced back through the leak point into the coil, resealing the system temporarily
The blower dilutes and disperses leaked refrigerant through the duct system so room concentration stays low
The blower run is a fault in itself, because mitigation design requires the air handler to shut down every moving part the instant a sensor trips

questions.explanation: Leak mitigation uses indoor airflow to dilute and disperse refrigerant so concentration in the occupied space stays low. The run is not a heat-strip cool-down, airflow cannot push vapor back into a leaking coil or reseal it, and the blower operation is an intended mitigation response rather than a second fault.

questions.question: A split air conditioner shows low suction pressure, a frost line forming at the evaporator outlet, low evaporator superheat, and a supply-to-return temperature split of 27°F. Airflow checks have not yet been done. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: An overcharge of refrigerant flooding the evaporator, with liquid stacking in the receiver and condenser
A dirty condenser coil raising the head pressure
Low indoor airflow across an under-loaded, excessively cold evaporator coil
Noncondensable gas trapped in the condenser

questions.explanation: Low airflow unloads the evaporator, dropping suction pressure and superheat while the reduced air volume picks up an abnormally large temperature split and the coil runs cold enough to frost. Option A would tend to raise suction pressure rather than lower it, and option B primarily raises head pressure instead of frosting the evaporator. Option D also drives head pressure up and does not explain the high temperature split.

questions.question: A furnace with a new flame sensor and a clean burner still drops out seconds after light-off intermittently. Flame signal fluctuates between 0.8 and 3 µA, gas pressure and sensor position are correct, and electrical checks find hot and neutral reversed at the furnace junction box (120 V from neutral to ground). What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A cracked heat exchanger, which disturbs flames and raises CO but does not reverse electrical polarity or make the microamp signal unstable
A weak gas valve coil dropping out under load, which would show manifold pressure collapsing at dropout rather than a fluctuating flame signal
A defective new flame sensor, which is unlikely because the signal fluctuates with the wiring fault and the sensor was just replaced with no change
Reversed polarity defeating flame rectification

questions.explanation: Flame rectification depends on correct polarity and grounding; reversed hot/neutral makes the sense signal weak and unstable even with a new sensor correctly positioned. The replacement sensor changed nothing, manifold pressure holds through dropout, and a cracked exchanger cannot produce the measured polarity reversal.

questions.question: A homeowner complains the heat pump 'stopped working' at 20 degrees F because supply air feels cool and run times are long, yet the house holds setpoint without auxiliary heat running excessively. What is the best explanation?

answers.text: The reversing valve must be leaking because supply air should feel as hot as a gas furnace
Heat pump capacity and supply-air temperature fall as outdoor temperature drops, so long run times with lukewarm air can be normal if setpoint is maintained
The system is in permanent defrost
The thermostat should force strip heat below 40 degrees F in all cases

questions.explanation: As outdoor temperature falls, a heat pump moves less heat and delivers cooler supply air, so long cycles that hold setpoint are expected behavior, option B. A leaking valve (A) would show capacity loss and failure to hold setpoint, permanent defrost (C) would fail to heat normally and cycle auxiliaries constantly, and forcing strips in all cases below 40 degrees (D) wastes energy when the heat pump is still carrying the load.

questions.question: Duct leakage results are reported at 25 Pa, about 0.10 in. w.c., even though operating duct pressures vary by location and system. Why is 25 Pa used?

answers.text: It is a standardized reference pressure
It is the exact pressure found at every register in every residential system, so test results at 25 Pa need no interpretation to reflect operating leakage rates
It is the highest pressure a residential duct can withstand, chosen so the test doubles as a structural proof test of the duct joints and seams
It is the pressure at which leakage stops changing with pressure, so readings taken there equal the leakage that occurs at any other operating pressure

questions.explanation: Twenty-five pascals is an agreed reference pressure that makes leakage results comparable between houses, testers, and before-and-after sealing work. Operating pressures vary widely and are not uniformly 25 Pa, residential ducts withstand far more than this gentle test pressure, and leakage does change with pressure, which is exactly why a fixed reference is needed.

questions.question: In an inverter air conditioner, what does the inverter section do after the incoming AC supply is rectified?

answers.text: Stores the DC permanently in a battery bank so the compressor can run during a utility outage without any generator connected to the system
Steps the DC down to thermostat voltage so the indoor control board and the compressor can share one low-voltage power supply safely
Synthesizes variable-frequency, variable-voltage AC, so compressor motor speed can be varied continuously with the load
Converts the DC back to fixed 60 Hz AC at a higher voltage, because the compressor motor is a standard single-speed induction design

questions.explanation: The drive rectifies line power to DC, then its inverter stage builds variable-frequency, variable-voltage AC to vary compressor speed. There is no battery storage for outage operation, the control board has its own low-voltage supply, and the output frequency varies rather than returning to fixed line frequency.

questions.question: A furnace clocks at an input 20% above its rating plate after a gas-valve replacement. The most likely setup causes are:

answers.text: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed
A vent connector one size larger than the minimum, because a larger vent increases draft and pulls extra gas through the burner orifices
A sediment trap with a long capped leg, because the trap volume adds a reserve of gas that the meter counts as additional furnace input
A thermostat set several degrees above room temperature, because a larger temperature difference makes the gas valve deliver more fuel per hour

questions.explanation: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed. Vent size, trap volume, and thermostat setting do not change firing rate; excessive manifold pressure or oversized orifices do.

questions.question: A CO alarm sounds in a home with gas appliances and occupants report headaches that ease outdoors. What is the correct immediate response?

answers.text: Open one window near the alarm, reset it to silence the alert, and stay in the house to see whether it sounds again over the next several hours
Turn the thermostat up to burn off the carbon monoxide
Leave the building, get fresh air, and call emergency services or the gas utility before re-entering
Run the kitchen exhaust for an hour while staying inside to monitor

questions.explanation: Symptoms plus an alarm call for evacuation and professional response, not troubleshooting in place. Resetting the alarm while staying inside prolongs exposure. Heating does not remove CO, and relying on a kitchen fan while remaining indoors leaves occupants at risk if levels are high.

questions.question: Why must a refrigerant cylinder never be heated with an open flame or filled beyond its rated capacity?

answers.text: It improves charging accuracy
Overfilling or heating can raise pressure to rupture, and flame can decompose refrigerant into toxic gases
It only affects the cylinder paint
Cylinders are designed for any pressure

questions.explanation: Heat and overfilling can raise cylinder pressure to rupture, and flame contact can create highly toxic decomposition products, so B is correct. A is false because these practices are dangerous, not helpful, C trivializes the hazard, and D contradicts cylinder pressure ratings.

questions.question: An 80% furnace is replaced with a 96% condensing furnace reusing the old B-vent chimney path. What venting change is required?

answers.text: The B-vent can be kept unchanged because furnace vent categories are interchangeable whenever the vent diameter stays the same
The old vent can be kept if the installer raises the flue temperature by removing the new furnace's secondary heat exchanger
The new furnace needs its listed plastic or approved vent system; its cool, condensing exhaust cannot use the old B-vent as-is
The chimney should be capped and the new furnace vented into the attic space, where its exhaust is too cool to cause any harm

questions.explanation: Condensing furnaces produce cool, wet exhaust that requires listed corrosion-resistant venting routed outdoors. Vent categories are not interchangeable by diameter, removing a heat exchanger is not an installation option, and exhaust must never terminate in an attic.

questions.question: A reach-in cooler shows high evaporator superheat, low subcooling, and bubbles in the liquid line sight glass, with a clean condenser and normal airflow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: The system is undercharged, so flash gas forms in the liquid line and the evaporator is starved
The system is overcharged, so excess liquid backs up in the condenser and floods the evaporator coil
The compressor valves are bypassing, so discharge gas leaks back and superheats the suction vapor
The evaporator fan is running backward, so air short-circuits the coil and leaves the refrigerant cold

questions.explanation: A is correct: too little charge means the liquid seal is lost, flash gas appears as bubbles in the sight glass, subcooling falls, and the starved evaporator produces high superheat. B is wrong because an overcharge raises subcooling and clears the sight glass, the opposite pattern. C is wrong because bypassing compressor valves cut capacity and raise suction pressure rather than producing low subcooling with a starved coil. D is wrong because an airflow fault frosts or ices the coil and tends to lower, not raise, the measured superheat pattern described.

delaware-hvac.quiz_title: Delaware HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: An evaporator has heavy frost building on the coil, low suction pressure, a warm conditioned space, and weak airflow from the registers. Inspection finds a very dirty air filter restricting air through the coil. The cause is most likely:

answers.text: An overcharge of refrigerant
A condenser fan running backwards
Low airflow across the evaporator, which drops coil temperature below freezing and builds frost that blocks airflow further
A liquid-line restriction after the filter drier that starves the evaporator, raises superheat, and reduces cooling in the last circuits of the coil downstream

questions.explanation: When airflow falls, the coil gets colder than designed, moisture freezes on it, and the frost insulates and blocks air in a worsening cycle while the space stays warm. An overcharge in option A tends to raise suction pressure, option B affects the condenser and head pressure, and option D would starve the coil and raise superheat rather than primarily cutting register airflow.

questions.question: A homeowner asks why the new R-454B air handler runs its blower for a while after a leak sensor trips, even though cooling has stopped. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The blower is removing residual heat from the electric heat strips, a normal cool-down sequence that happens to coincide with the sensor alarm event
The blower pressurizes the duct system so refrigerant vapor is forced back through the leak point into the coil, resealing the system temporarily
The blower dilutes and disperses leaked refrigerant through the duct system so room concentration stays low
The blower run is a fault in itself, because mitigation design requires the air handler to shut down every moving part the instant a sensor trips

questions.explanation: Leak mitigation uses indoor airflow to dilute and disperse refrigerant so concentration in the occupied space stays low. The run is not a heat-strip cool-down, airflow cannot push vapor back into a leaking coil or reseal it, and the blower operation is an intended mitigation response rather than a second fault.

questions.question: Where is a fuel deaerator typically installed, and what must its vent or return arrangement do?

answers.text: Inside the oil tank itself, submerged in fuel, where it vents air bubbles directly into the stored oil for reabsorption later
On the burner fuel unit discharge, where it stores high-pressure oil to smooth nozzle pressure pulses during ignition trials
In the flue pipe, where exhaust heat boils air out of the oil before the oil returns through the chimney to the tank top
Near the burner, venting separated air safely

questions.explanation: A deaerator mounts near the burner on the supply line, separating air and vapor and venting or returning them safely so only de-aerated oil reaches the pump. Option A submerges a device that must vent air out of the fuel, option B misplaces it on the pressure side as an accumulator, and option C invents a flue-mounted oil path.

questions.question: A technician sets the closed-position stop on non-calling zone dampers so each blade leaks a small amount of air instead of sealing fully. What is the purpose, and the cost?

answers.text: The leak prevents damper blades from sticking after long idle periods, and its cost is the motor wear caused by the panel driving the blades against the stop repeatedly
The bleed relieves some excess pressure, at the cost of conditioning zones that are not calling
The leak equalizes humidity between zones, and its cost is that satisfied zones slowly take on the moisture load of calling zones through the shared return system
The bleed raises total airflow so the smallest zone can be served without a bypass, and its cost is that the equipment must be oversized for the whole house to feed the leakage

questions.explanation: Leaving non-calling dampers slightly open gives excess air additional paths, which trims static pressure when few zones call. The trade-off is real: satisfied zones receive conditioned air they did not ask for, while blade sticking, humidity transfer, and equipment sizing are not the purpose or the cost of the setting.

questions.question: A 24 V contactor coil measures 15 ohms. Using Ohm's law, about how much current does the coil draw when energized?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law gives I = V/R = 24/15 = 1.6 A. Dividing resistance by voltage inverts the formula and gives 0.63. Adding or multiplying voltage and resistance produces values far beyond what a small control coil draws.

questions.question: A long liquid line is one size too small for the load. The most likely operating symptom is:

answers.text: No symptom, because liquid lines cannot have pressure drop no matter how small the tubing, how long the run, or how many elbows, valves, and vertical lifts are installed between the receiver and the expansion device
Oil logging in the liquid line riser
Excessive pressure drop that consumes subcooling and can flash liquid to vapor before the expansion valve, reducing its capacity
A suction line that sweats heavily indoors

questions.explanation: Undersized liquid piping creates friction pressure drop; if drop plus lift consumes the available subcooling, flash gas forms ahead of the valve and starves it. Option A denies basic friction loss, option B misplaces oil logging, which is a low-velocity suction problem, and option D describes suction-line condensation, not a liquid-line sizing effect.

questions.question: Where does a fan-powered humidifier belong, and why does placement matter?

answers.text: In the return drop only, because fan-powered models depend entirely on the return airstream being warmer than the supply airstream
Loose in the blower compartment, where unducted air movement across the panel provides enough evaporation for a whole house
On the outdoor condensing unit, where weather provides airflow and the moisture can be piped indoors with the refrigerant lines
On the supply plenum, where its own fan pushes air through the water panel independent of bypass duct pressure differences.

questions.explanation: A fan-powered unit is a supply-plenum appliance with its own fan, so it does not rely on supply-to-return pressure difference like a bypass model. It is not a return-only or loose-in-cabinet device, and humidification is an indoor air-side function, not an outdoor refrigerant-side one.

questions.question: In January a house shows heavy window condensation and RH of 55% indoors at 70°F, with no plumbing or roof leaks found. What is the most likely explanation?

answers.text: Outdoor winter air leaking in is humidifying the house, because cold outdoor air holds more moisture than warm indoor air and releases it at the windows
The windows are defective and are generating moisture at the glass, which is why condensation appears there first instead of anywhere else in the rooms
The furnace humidifier has failed empty and is somehow adding moisture, since window condensation in winter is a standard symptom of too little indoor humidity
Indoor vapor condensing on cold glass

questions.explanation: At 55% RH the indoor dew point is high enough that cold window glass falls below it, so indoor-generated vapor condenses on the coldest surface. Winter outdoor air is dry and dilutes indoor moisture when it leaks in, glass does not generate moisture, and a failed-empty humidifier would lower rather than raise indoor humidity.

questions.question: The same model of air conditioner is being selected for two identical houses, one near sea level and one at about 6,000 feet elevation. Why can't the designer simply use the same airflow and capacity assumptions for both?

answers.text: At elevation the air is less dense, so each cubic foot carries less heat: the system needs more CFM to move the same heat, and rated capacities and combustion appliance inputs must be corrected for the thinner air

At elevation air is denser, so airflow should be reduced by the same percentage, because each cubic foot delivered at altitude carries more heat than it would at sea level and the coil therefore needs less volume moving across it in both heating and cooling operation
Elevation affects only heating equipment, never cooling airflow
Standard sea-level tables already include an automatic altitude correction

questions.explanation: Density falls with altitude, and both heat transport by air and manufacturer capacity ratings are stated for standard-density air, so design values must be adjusted. Option B is wrong because density decreases, not increases, with elevation — the correction runs the opposite direction; option C is wrong because cooling coils move heat with air, so cooling airflow is directly affected by density; option D is wrong because published ratings assume standard air; altitude corrections are a separate designer step, not built in.

questions.question: A condensate drain line is installed dead level for a long run and plugs with slime every season. What installation defect is most likely?

answers.text: The line was made from approved drain material instead of thin-wall tubing that stays warmer and therefore resists biological growth
The drain terminates at an approved receptor instead of discharging directly onto the roof membrane below the condensing unit
The trap was installed at the unit rather than at the far end of the run near the floor drain, where traps are most effective
The line lacks continuous downward slope in the direction of flow.

questions.explanation: Condensate drains must fall continuously, about an eighth inch per foot, so water and debris do not stand in the line. Approved material and an approved receptor are correct practice, not defects, and the trap belongs at the unit to prevent air issues.

questions.question: A variable-speed drive slows a chilled-water pump to 90% of full speed. Using the pump affinity laws, about how much pump power is saved?

answers.text: About 3%, because pump power falls only in direct one-to-one proportion to the drop in pump rotational speed
About 10%, because pump power falls in proportion to the square of the speed ratio at reduced flow conditions
About 19%, because pump head and pump power always change by exactly the same percentage as each other
About 27%, because power varies with the cube of speed: 0.9 cubed is about 0.73 of full power

questions.explanation: Power follows the cube law: 0.9^3 = 0.729, so roughly 27% of the power is saved. Option A uses the flow relationship, option B uses the head (square) relationship, and option C wrongly equates head and power changes, which follow different exponents.

questions.question: A gas furnace in Bear lights its burners on every call for heat, but the burners shut off again after only a few seconds, cycle after cycle, while the inducer keeps running normally. The flame sensor rod is visibly coated with a white oxide film. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: The coated sensor cannot pass an adequate flame-rectification signal to the control, so the board shuts the gas valve down when it fails to prove flame

The oxide film makes the sensor read too much flame current, so the board opens the valve wider until the high limit trips the burners off, after which the board advances the inducer to high speed and holds the furnace in a permanent heating lockout
The flame sensor controls the inducer motor speed, and its coating has slowed the inducer below the pressure switch setpoint
The coating insulates the sensor so well that the board believes the heat exchanger is overheated and locks the furnace out for one hour

questions.explanation: A is correct: the control proves flame by the small rectified current the flame carries to the sensor rod; an oxide coating insulates the rod and drops that signal, so the board closes the gas valve seconds after ignition. Cleaning the rod restores the signal. B is wrong because a coated sensor reduces flame current rather than increasing it, and the board does not modulate the valve from it. C is wrong because the flame sensor plays no part in inducer speed or pressure-switch operation. D is wrong because flame proving, not exchanger temperature, is the sensor's function, and the symptom timing matches a failed flame proof.
