questions.question: An evaporator has heavy frost building on the coil, low suction pressure, a warm conditioned space, and weak airflow from the registers. Inspection finds a very dirty air filter restricting air through the coil. The cause is most likely:

answers.text: An overcharge of refrigerant
A condenser fan running backwards
Low airflow across the evaporator, which drops coil temperature below freezing and builds frost that blocks airflow further
A liquid-line restriction after the filter drier that starves the evaporator, raises superheat, and reduces cooling in the last circuits of the coil downstream

questions.explanation: When airflow falls, the coil gets colder than designed, moisture freezes on it, and the frost insulates and blocks air in a worsening cycle while the space stays warm. An overcharge in option A tends to raise suction pressure, option B affects the condenser and head pressure, and option D would starve the coil and raise superheat rather than primarily cutting register airflow.

questions.question: A homeowner asks why the new R-454B air handler runs its blower for a while after a leak sensor trips, even though cooling has stopped. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The blower is removing residual heat from the electric heat strips, a normal cool-down sequence that happens to coincide with the sensor alarm event
The blower pressurizes the duct system so refrigerant vapor is forced back through the leak point into the coil, resealing the system temporarily
The blower dilutes and disperses leaked refrigerant through the duct system so room concentration stays low
The blower run is a fault in itself, because mitigation design requires the air handler to shut down every moving part the instant a sensor trips

questions.explanation: Leak mitigation uses indoor airflow to dilute and disperse refrigerant so concentration in the occupied space stays low. The run is not a heat-strip cool-down, airflow cannot push vapor back into a leaking coil or reseal it, and the blower operation is an intended mitigation response rather than a second fault.

questions.question: A TXV system in cooling mode has normal evaporator superheat, both pressures somewhat high, and subcooling of 24°F against a manufacturer target of 10°F. Cooling capacity is slightly reduced. What condition best fits these readings?

answers.text: Overcharge, with excess liquid backing up in the condenser
Undercharge, with the condenser only partly filled with liquid
A restricted liquid-line filter drier starving the TXV
Low indoor airflow across the evaporator coil

questions.explanation: With a TXV holding superheat steady, excess charge collects in the condenser and shows up as abnormally high subcooling with elevated pressures. Option B is the opposite condition and would produce low subcooling, while option C starves the valve and raises superheat rather than holding it normal. Option D lowers suction pressure and superheat, which does not match the normal superheat reading here.

questions.question: At a furnace install, a flexible gas connector is routed through a hole in the furnace cabinet side to reach the gas valve. What is wrong with this?

answers.text: Connectors must not pass through the cabinet
Flexible connectors are prohibited on all furnaces, so the entire run from the meter must be flexible line without rigid pipe
The connector is too visible for inspection, and routing it through the cabinet is preferred so it is hidden from view at all times
Nothing is wrong, provided the hole is left sharp and unbushed so the connector is gripped tightly and cannot move in service

questions.explanation: A flexible connector must not pass through the appliance cabinet, wall, or floor; rigid pipe penetrates the cabinet and the connector joins outside it. Option B reverses the rule, since connectors are permitted within their listing and length limits, option C values concealment over a clear prohibition, and option D adds an abrasion hazard at a sharp edge.

questions.question: A 96% AFUE furnace is installed in a basement. Its flue gases are relatively cool and the vent system is designed to operate under positive pressure with a condensate drain at the furnace. How should its venting be handled?

answers.text: Vent it into an existing unlined masonry chimney with no corrosion-resistant liner, relying on the chimney's natural draft to carry the cool flue gases out
Use a single-wall metal connector into a Type B vent shared with a water heater
Vent it with the manufacturer-approved sealed plastic vent system and drain the condensate as directed
Let it vent into the basement and rely on dilution air to carry products out

questions.explanation: A 96% unit is a condensing, positive-pressure (Category IV) appliance, so it needs the manufacturer-approved sealed vent material and condensate handling in option C. Cool, moisture-laden flue gas would condense in and damage an unlined masonry chimney (A), Type B/common venting (B) is for negative-pressure non-condensing appliances and risks spillage, and venting into the space (D) is a carbon-monoxide hazard.

questions.question: Return ducts leak in a dusty attic and the house seems dustier with a slight negative pressure effect on a water heater. Why is return leakage especially concerning?

answers.text: It only wastes a little cool air
It pulls unfiltered attic air and contaminants into the system and can depressurize the home
It improves indoor air quality
It lowers humidity in all cases

questions.explanation: Return-side leaks entrain unfiltered, hot, dusty attic air, add load, and can contribute to depressurization that affects combustion appliances, so B is correct. A understates the harm, C is opposite, and D is false because attic air often adds moisture.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a heat anticipator in a traditional electromechanical thermostat?

answers.text: To open the heating contacts slightly early to prevent temperature overshoot from residual heat
To increase the furnace firing rate automatically whenever outdoor temperature falls below a set balance point during cold weather
To delay the blower until the heat exchanger is fully hot
To add resistance so the thermostat can operate without a common wire

questions.explanation: The anticipator warms the sensing element so contacts open before residual heat overshoots the setpoint, which is correct. Increasing firing rate is a burner control function, not the anticipator. Blower delay is handled by a fan control or board timing, not the anticipator. Operating without a common wire relates to power-stealing or batteries, not anticipation.

questions.question: A furnace clocks at an input 20% above its rating plate after a gas-valve replacement. The most likely setup causes are:

answers.text: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed
A vent connector one size larger than the minimum, because a larger vent increases draft and pulls extra gas through the burner orifices
A sediment trap with a long capped leg, because the trap volume adds a reserve of gas that the meter counts as additional furnace input
A thermostat set several degrees above room temperature, because a larger temperature difference makes the gas valve deliver more fuel per hour

questions.explanation: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed. Vent size, trap volume, and thermostat setting do not change firing rate; excessive manifold pressure or oversized orifices do.

questions.question: On a cold morning a water heater spills briefly at the draft hood for the first minute after firing, then establishes steady draft and spills no more. The flue is clear and zone pressure is near neutral. What best fits this pattern?

answers.text: Cold flue with delayed draft
A blocked flue, which characteristically spills only at startup and then clears itself completely once the burner has run for about a minute
A cracked heat exchanger in the nearby furnace, which pushes flue gas out of the water heater hood only while both appliances start at the same time
Excessive combustion-appliance zone depressurization, which is known to disappear on its own as soon as the burner warms regardless of exhaust operation

questions.explanation: A cold flue has little initial draft, so brief startup spillage that clears as the chimney warms fits a cold-flue, delayed-draft pattern. A blocked flue spills persistently rather than clearing, a furnace heat-exchanger crack does not produce this timed water-heater pattern, and depressurization-driven spillage continues while the exhaust load continues instead of resolving with warm-up.

questions.question: A meter shows a capacitor in a de-energized unit still holding charge. What should the technician do before handling its terminals?

answers.text: Touch both terminals together with bare fingers to drain off the stored charge as quickly as possible
Safely discharge the capacitor through an appropriate resistor and verify zero volts
Assume it drained because power is off
Hit it with a screwdriver handle

questions.explanation: Capacitors store charge after power is removed and must be discharged through a suitable resistor and verified at zero volts, so B is correct. Touching terminals risks shock and burns, assuming drainage is unsafe, and striking the part can damage it and still leave charge.

questions.question: A homeowner finished a 400-square-foot addition served by the existing system and now wants a changeout. What design step is required before selecting equipment?

answers.text: A new load calculation covering the enlarged conditioned space, rather than sizing from the original home alone
No calculation, because additions under 500 square feet are absorbed by the safety factor built into every residential system
Sizing by the addition's square footage at the same tons-per-square-foot ratio the original installer used decades ago
Selecting equipment one full ton larger than the old unit, which reliably covers any addition of this general size

questions.explanation: Added conditioned area changes the load and the room-by-room distribution, so a fresh calculation must include it. There is no automatic safety factor for additions, rules of thumb repeat old errors, and a flat one-ton bump is unrelated to the actual load.

questions.question: A boiler room in a New Haven building contains fuel-fired appliances with a combined input of 160,000 Btu/h, and the contractor wants to rely on the indoor-air standard method for combustion air. The room as built measures 7,500 cubic feet. What does the method require here?

answers.text: The room is unconfined, because the standard method needs only 25 cubic feet per 1,000 Btu/h, which gives 160 x 25 = 4,000 cubic feet for this combined input rating and plenty of margin.
More room volume or another combustion-air method: the standard method needs 50 cubic feet per 1,000 Btu/h, so 160 x 50 = 8,000 cubic feet, and a 7,500-cubic-foot room leaves the space confined.
The room is unconfined no matter what its volume is, because indoor air may always be used when the appliances sit in a room whose door can simply be left open during firing.
The volume is sufficient if only the largest single appliance is counted instead of the combined input, because the indoor method is applied appliance by appliance in a shared room.

questions.explanation: B is correct: under the standard indoor-air method a space is unconfined only at 50 cubic feet of volume per 1,000 Btu/h of combined input; 160,000 Btu/h requires 160 x 50 = 8,000 cubic feet, so 7,500 cubic feet is a confined space needing a combustion-air remedy. A is wrong because the standard-method ratio is 50 cubic feet per 1,000 Btu/h, not 25. C is wrong because an open door does not change the space's calculated volume or make a confined space unconfined. D is wrong because the volume calculation uses the combined input of all fuel-fired appliances in the space, not the largest one alone.

arizona-hvac.quiz_title: Arizona HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: A standard cooling rating point uses hot outdoor conditions. As outdoor temperature climbs well above that point on an extreme afternoon, what happens to a fixed-speed system's capacity and power draw?

answers.text: Capacity climbs steadily with outdoor temperature because the compressor pumps refrigerant faster as discharge pressure rises against the hotter condenser airstream
Power draw falls to its seasonal minimum at extreme temperatures, which is exactly why utilities schedule demand charges around mild-weather operating hours instead
Capacity falls while power draw generally rises
Both capacity and power stay locked at their rating-point values, because nameplate ratings are guaranteed performance figures at every outdoor temperature a system may face

questions.explanation: Hotter condensing conditions raise the pressure lift the compressor works against, so it moves less refrigerant, delivers less capacity, and draws more power doing it. Capacity does not climb with head pressure, extreme heat is the high-draw condition rather than the minimum, and ratings describe one test point rather than a guarantee at all temperatures.

questions.question: A rooftop evaporative cooler in Yuma delivers 4,000 cfm through a pad bank with 16 square feet of face area. What is the air velocity through the pads?

answers.text: 64,000 feet per minute, because the airflow is multiplied by the pad area instead of being divided by it to find the face velocity
125 feet per minute, because the airflow is divided by 32 square feet, double the pad face area actually fitted to this cooler cabinet
250 feet per minute, because 4,000 cfm divided by the 16 square feet of pad face area gives the velocity at which air crosses the media
500 feet per minute, because the airflow is divided by 8 square feet, treating only half the pad bank as active during normal operation

questions.explanation: C is correct: face velocity equals airflow divided by face area, so 4,000 divided by 16 equals 250 feet per minute across the pads. A is wrong because multiplying airflow by area inverts the relationship and produces a meaningless figure. B is wrong because it doubles the pad area, halving the velocity. D is wrong because it halves the pad area on the assumption that only part of the bank is active, doubling the velocity.

questions.question: In a conventional dual-fuel installation with a gas furnace below an indoor coil, why must the control be interlocked so the furnace and the heat pump do not deliver their full heating at the same time through that coil arrangement?

answers.text: Simultaneous full operation can send furnace-heated air through the indoor coil while it is acting as a condenser, driving refrigerant pressures and temperatures beyond design limits
The furnace and heat pump together would use less energy than either one alone
The thermostat cannot display two heat sources on its screen at once
The gas valve and reversing valve share a single wire that can carry only one signal

questions.explanation: With the coil downstream of the furnace, furnace heat added to a coil that is already condensing refrigerant in heat pump heating can push head pressure and discharge temperature too high, so dual-fuel controls select one source. Option B states an efficiency outcome backwards, option C is a display concern, not an operating limit, and option D invents a wiring limit instead of the refrigerant-side reason.

questions.question: A natural gas furnace is being converted to propane with the correct kit. Why are the propane burner orifices smaller than the natural gas orifices they replace?

answers.text: Smaller orifices compensate for propane being a weaker fuel per cubic foot, by forcing the gas valve to stay open longer on each heating cycle than it did on natural gas
Propane is richer per cubic foot and is supplied at higher manifold pressure
Smaller orifices are used only to slow the gas meter, because propane is billed by orifice size rather than by the volume or weight of fuel actually delivered
Propane orifices are smaller because propane burners must run at a much lower input than the nameplate rating, typically about half the natural gas input for the same furnace

questions.explanation: Propane carries more heat per cubic foot and is burned at a higher manifold pressure, so a smaller opening passes the volume needed for the rated input. Using the larger natural gas opening would overfire the furnace, and the goal is the same nameplate input, not a longer cycle, a slower meter, or half rating.

questions.question: Supply ducts in a hot attic leak 15% of airflow. Which effect is most direct?

answers.text: Rooms receive more air than designed
Delivered capacity falls and run time and energy use rise
Static pressure in the rooms increases
Refrigerant charge automatically increases to compensate for the lost supply airflow

questions.explanation: Leaked supply air never reaches the rooms, so delivered capacity falls and the system runs longer using more energy, making B correct. A is opposite to the loss, room static does not rise from supply leakage, and duct leakage has no automatic effect on refrigerant charge.

questions.question: Line voltages at a motor read 232 V, 238 V, and 241 V. The average is about 237 V and the greatest deviation is about 5 V. The voltage imbalance is about:

answers.text: 7%, found by adding the three deviations from nominal nameplate voltage together instead of comparing the greatest deviation with the average voltage
12%, found by dividing the highest line voltage by the lowest line voltage and reporting the difference between the two readings as a percentage
0.2%, found by moving the decimal on the deviation in volts and treating that number directly as the percentage imbalance for the motor supply

questions.explanation: The voltage imbalance is about 2%. Imbalance is greatest deviation divided by average, about 5/237 or roughly 2%; the other figures come from the stated calculation errors.

questions.question: New steel gas piping for a Phoenix restaurant will operate well under 1 psig. What minimum test pressure does the fuel gas code require for the pressure test before the line is put in service?

answers.text: A test equal to the proposed working pressure, held just long enough to read the gauge once
A test of 1 psig, because low-pressure systems are exempt from any higher minimum test pressure
At least 1.5 times the proposed maximum working pressure, and in no case less than 3 psig
A test of 60 psig on every system, because the code sets one fixed test pressure for all gas piping

questions.explanation: C is correct: the fuel gas code requires the test pressure to be at least one and one-half times the proposed maximum working pressure, with a floor of 3 psig regardless of how low the working pressure is. A is wrong because testing at working pressure alone does not meet the one-and-one-half-times requirement. B is wrong because the 3 psig minimum applies precisely to low-pressure systems like this one. D is wrong because the code sets a proportional test with a floor, not a single fixed pressure for all piping.

questions.question: A furnace clocks at an input 20% above its rating plate after a gas-valve replacement. The most likely setup causes are:

answers.text: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed
A vent connector one size larger than the minimum, because a larger vent increases draft and pulls extra gas through the burner orifices
A sediment trap with a long capped leg, because the trap volume adds a reserve of gas that the meter counts as additional furnace input
A thermostat set several degrees above room temperature, because a larger temperature difference makes the gas valve deliver more fuel per hour

questions.explanation: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed. Vent size, trap volume, and thermostat setting do not change firing rate; excessive manifold pressure or oversized orifices do.

questions.question: The longest measured duct path in a design is 92 feet from the plenum to the farthest register. The fittings on that path have a combined equivalent length of 58 feet. What total effective length (TEL) is used in the friction-rate calculation?

answers.text: 92 feet, because fittings are already included in the measured length
34 feet, the measured length minus the fittings' equivalent length
150 feet, the measured length plus the fittings' equivalent length
58 feet, because the fittings dominate and the straight length can be dropped

questions.explanation: TEL converts every fitting into the length of straight duct that would cause the same pressure drop and adds it to the measured run: 92 + 58 = 150 feet. Option A is wrong because measured length is tape-measure distance only; fitting losses are separate and must be added; option B is wrong because subtracting would claim the fittings help the airflow, when every fitting adds resistance; option D is wrong because straight duct friction is real and usually the larger share; dropping it understates TEL and oversizes the friction rate.

questions.question: A flex duct run to a new air handler sags between supports and is compressed where it turns. What is the correct installation fix?

answers.text: Leave the sag, because flex duct is rated with sag included and its airflow equals rigid duct of the same nominal size
Compress the run further at the turn to raise air velocity and compensate for the friction added by the sagging sections
Support it at proper intervals and make gentle, fully extended turns so the inner core keeps its full diameter
Replace the flex with a smaller diameter so the blower's higher pressure can force the same airflow through the restriction

questions.explanation: Sagging and crushed turns add major friction; proper support and full extension preserve rated airflow. Flex ratings assume correct installation rather than sag, deliberate compression raises resistance instead of compensating, and downsizing the duct worsens the same problem.

questions.question: A variable-speed drive slows a chilled-water pump to 90% of full speed. Using the pump affinity laws, about how much pump power is saved?

answers.text: About 3%, because pump power falls only in direct one-to-one proportion to the drop in pump rotational speed
About 10%, because pump power falls in proportion to the square of the speed ratio at reduced flow conditions
About 19%, because pump head and pump power always change by exactly the same percentage as each other
About 27%, because power varies with the cube of speed: 0.9 cubed is about 0.73 of full power

questions.explanation: Power follows the cube law: 0.9^3 = 0.729, so roughly 27% of the power is saved. Option A uses the flow relationship, option B uses the head (square) relationship, and option C wrongly equates head and power changes, which follow different exponents.

questions.question: A contractor holds only a CR-39 license and is offered a commercial rooftop replacement and, separately, a residential split-system changeout, neither involving solar equipment. What does the license authorize?

answers.text: Only the residential job, because the dual designation in this family is built on the residential license and commercial work needs a separate C-39
Neither job until the contractor also passes the solar portion, because every dual license in the family is conditioned on solar qualification
Both jobs, because the dual no-solar license allows the scopes of both the commercial C-39 and the residential R-39R licenses
Only the commercial job, because dual licenses in this family pair a commercial class with a temperature-control subclass rather than a residential class

questions.explanation: C is correct: a CR-39 license allows the scopes of work permitted by both the C-39 commercial license and the R-39R residential license, so both non-solar jobs are within the one dual license. A is wrong because the dual license is not residential-only. B is wrong because the CR-39 is the no-solar dual class and carries no solar-portion condition. D is wrong because the pairing is commercial plus residential, not commercial plus a subclass.

arkansas-hvac.quiz_title: Arkansas HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: A technician checks a liquid-line sight glass with a moisture indicator on a system that is fully charged and has adequate subcooling. The glass is clear but the indicator shows the color for wet. What should the technician conclude?

answers.text: The charge is low because the glass is clear
Moisture is present in the system, so the filter drier should be replaced and the source of moisture investigated
The system must be overcharged
The sight glass proves the refrigerant is the wrong type because its color and clarity can identify the chemical composition of any blend in the system

questions.explanation: With charge and subcooling already confirmed, a wet indication points to moisture contamination, addressed by replacing the drier and finding how moisture entered. Option A contradicts the confirmed charge, option C would not change the moisture indicator to wet, and option D is wrong because a sight glass does not identify refrigerant type.

questions.question: A system cools the air temperature adequately but humidity stays near 65%. Readings: airflow measured at 485 cfm/ton, air-side temperature split only 13°F, superheat 9°F, subcooling 10°F, pressures normal, coil clean, and condensate barely drips except on the hottest afternoons. What adjustment does the evidence support?

answers.text: Install a larger evaporator coil, a major change that does nothing about air moving too fast for moisture to condense on the coil surface
Increase blower speed further to move more air across the coil, which would raise coil temperature even more and strip off still less moisture
Add refrigerant to drop the suction pressure and coil temperature, which would corrupt the currently correct superheat and subcooling values
Reduce blower speed to lower airflow per ton

questions.explanation: Excessive airflow per ton keeps the coil too warm and the split too small for sustained condensation, which the 13°F split and 485 cfm/ton prove. Slowing the blower lowers coil temperature and lengthens moisture contact; speeding it up worsens the problem, adding charge falsifies good readings, and a bigger coil does not fix air velocity.

questions.question: A PVC vent joint was dry-fitted, marked, and then assembled without primer or cement on one socket. It separates during the first heating season. What practice failure caused this?

answers.text: The installer used Schedule 40 pipe instead of a thinner-wall pipe that would have expanded more and locked the joint tightly
The joint was never solvent-welded
The installer failed to pressure-test the vent with high-pressure shop air, which is what normally fuses PVC joints together in place
The pipe was cut square instead of at an angle, so the cement had no wedge surface to grip as the fitting was pushed home fully

questions.explanation: PVC vent joints seal and hold only when they are properly primed and solvent-cemented; a dry-fitted socket has no bond and can pull apart. Option A is wrong because wall thickness does not create the joint, option C invents air-pressure fusing, and option D misstates cutting practice, since square cuts with full insertion are desired.

questions.question: On a spring-return zone damper, what happens when panel power to the damper motor is removed?

answers.text: The blade locks at whatever angle it held when power stopped, because the gear train cannot move in either direction without motor torque applied to the shaft
The blade drives fully closed at motor speed, because removing power reverses the motor through a capacitor stored in the damper actuator housing
A spring drives the blade back to its rest position, open or closed by design
The blade floats freely and follows duct pressure, swinging to whichever position the airflow in that branch happens to push it during the equipment cycle

questions.explanation: A spring-return actuator is motor driven in one direction and spring driven back to its designed rest position when power is removed, which is how its fail position is chosen. It does not lock in place, reverse electrically on stored charge, or float freely with duct pressure.

questions.question: A 24 V contactor coil measures 15 ohms. Using Ohm's law, about how much current does the coil draw when energized?
questions.explanation: Ohm's law gives I = V/R = 24/15 = 1.6 A. Dividing resistance by voltage inverts the formula and gives 0.63. Adding or multiplying voltage and resistance produces values far beyond what a small control coil draws.

questions.question: CSST runs through a house with several metal systems. The bonding jumper for the CSST is installed primarily to:

answers.text: Carry the normal return current of the HVAC circuits, so that a separate equipment grounding conductor is no longer needed for the furnace
Replace the grounding electrode conductor for the whole house, because bonding the gas tubing satisfies every grounding requirement by itself
Equalize electrical potential and reduce arcing damage from induced voltage
Prevent corrosion of the tubing by draining stray direct current from the gas line into the soil outside the building foundation wall

questions.explanation: Equalize electrical potential and reduce arcing damage from induced voltage. Bonding does not carry circuit return current, replace the service grounding system, or serve as a corrosion drain to soil.

questions.question: A tall suction riser is piped with no intermediate traps, and the compressor gradually loses oil that is found spread through the riser and evaporator. The piping correction is to:

answers.text: Remove the trap at the base of the riser as well
Slope the entire riser backward toward the evaporator, so any oil carried partway up the vertical run drains away from the compressor and collects in the coil whenever the system cycles off at night
Fill the riser halfway with oil before start-up
Add traps at the base and at intervals up the tall riser so oil is lifted in stages rather than having to climb the full height at once

questions.explanation: Intermediate traps break a tall lift into stages, collecting oil and letting gas carry it upward step by step instead of falling back. Removing the base trap in option A worsens drainage control, sloping toward the evaporator in option B sends oil away from the compressor, and option C overfills piping with oil that belongs in the crankcase.

questions.question: An ERV's measured outdoor airflow has fallen 25% over a year while fan energy has risen, and the wheel still rotates freely. What is the most likely service finding?

answers.text: The wheel has absorbed so much moisture that it has become heavier, and drying it with a heat gun restores the original airflow, a drying service the manufacturer supposedly recommends performing at every seasonal changeover without exception
Loaded filters and a fouled energy-transfer core are raising pressure drop, so the fans move less air against the added resistance
The exhaust and supply fans have exchanged rotation directions, which always shows up gradually over about a year's operation
The outdoor-air intake has grown larger through damper wear, letting in more air than the flow station was designed to measure

questions.explanation: Fouled media and filters are the routine cause of creeping pressure drop, falling airflow, and rising fan work. Option A proposes a drying procedure for a symptom fouling explains better, option C describes a wiring fault that would appear suddenly, not gradually, and option D claims more intake area reduces measured flow, which is the opposite of the finding.

questions.question: An appliance in an attic is reached through a small scuttle with no walkway and no lighting. Which condition must be corrected?

answers.text: Move the appliance disconnect to the living room so the technician never needs to enter the attic for any service operation
Provide a safe passageway, a service platform where required, lighting, and a receptacle at the appliance.
Require the homeowner to supply a flashlight and a loose sheet of plywood each time a technician visits the property
Enlarge the scuttle only if the appliance is replaced, because access rules apply solely on the day of original installation

questions.explanation: Technicians must be able to reach and service the appliance safely, with passage, platform, light, and power. A remote disconnect does not make the attic workable, borrowed plywood and flashlights are not permanent access, and access requirements are not waived between replacements.

questions.question: A dry-charge style replacement strategy is proposed: keep the R-22 coil and lines and install the least new equipment possible. What practical constraint should the contractor flag?

answers.text: Remaining R-22 components are aging together, unlisted for the new pairing, and dependent on scarce refrigerant for any future leak
There is no constraint, because partial R-22 replacements carry the same warranty and rating as a full matched system changeout
Keeping R-22 equipment guarantees lower operating cost for the next twenty years because the refrigerant is being phased out
The old coil will gain capacity each year as R-22 becomes scarcer, offsetting its age and corrosion in a predictable way

questions.explanation: Partial R-22 strategies inherit aged, unlisted components and exposure to scarce, costly refrigerant. They do not carry matched-system ratings or equivalent warranty, phaseout raises rather than lowers long-run cost, and scarcity does not add coil capacity.

questions.question: A variable-speed drive slows a chilled-water pump to 90% of full speed. Using the pump affinity laws, about how much pump power is saved?

answers.text: About 3%, because pump power falls only in direct one-to-one proportion to the drop in pump rotational speed
About 10%, because pump power falls in proportion to the square of the speed ratio at reduced flow conditions
About 19%, because pump head and pump power always change by exactly the same percentage as each other
About 27%, because power varies with the cube of speed: 0.9 cubed is about 0.73 of full power

questions.explanation: Power follows the cube law: 0.9^3 = 0.729, so roughly 27% of the power is saved. Option A uses the flow relationship, option B uses the head (square) relationship, and option C wrongly equates head and power changes, which follow different exponents.

questions.question: A draw-through air handler in Morrilton (blower downstream of the coil, so the drain pan sits under negative pressure) leaves its condensate pan full of standing water that spills at start-up, even though the drain line itself is clear and sloped. What is missing at the drain outlet?

answers.text: A check valve in the drain line, because condensate must be prevented from ever moving backward toward the air handler
A properly built trap, because without its water seal the negative pressure holds water in the pan and air up the line
A vent stack taller than the air handler, because condensate drains only when the line is vented like a plumbing fixture
A smaller drain line, because reducing the pipe size raises the water velocity enough to pull the pan completely dry

questions.explanation: B is correct: on a draw-through unit the drain pan is under negative pressure, and a trap's water seal stops air from being drawn up the drain line, which otherwise holds condensate in the pan until it overflows. A is wrong because a check valve is not the fitting that counters negative pressure at the pan. C is wrong because condensate drainage is governed by the trap seal and slope, not by a tall vent stack. D is wrong because a smaller line restricts drainage further and cannot overcome the pressure holding water in the pan.

maryland-hvac.quiz_title: Maryland HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: A compressor will not start after a long off period in a cold equipment room. The crankcase heater is found open-circuit, the oil sight glass shows a high, foamy level, and the compressor draws locked-rotor current briefly before tripping. What follow-up is most appropriate before returning it to regular service?

answers.text: Immediately add a full supplemental oil charge, because a foamy sight glass always means the crankcase is low on oil and needs additional volume right away
Replace the expansion valve with a smaller one, because migration during the off cycle is controlled entirely by the size of the valve orifice at the evaporator
Jumper the overload and force several long runs, because sustained running under load is the fastest way to prove the compressor has not been damaged by liquid
Restore the heater, warm and clear the oil of refrigerant, and verify oil condition before normal operation

questions.explanation: A dead heater allowed migration, so the heater must be restored and the refrigerant boiled out of the oil gently, with oil condition checked, before trusting the machine. A foamy glass reflects refrigerant in the oil, not a low oil charge needing more oil, migration is driven by temperature differences rather than expansion-valve orifice size, and forcing runs with an overload jumper risks destroying a possibly liquid-damaged compressor.

questions.question: A belt-drive blower motor draws nameplate amps at its current sheave setting. A proposal would raise blower speed by 10 percent to gain airflow. What should the contractor verify before approving the change?

answers.text: Only that a longer belt is in stock, because a 10 percent speed change is small enough that motor loading can be assumed unchanged for planning purposes
That the motor has reserve capacity, since power rises about 33 percent
That the supply registers are adjustable, because register dampers alone can absorb any extra motor load created by the faster blower speed setting
That the thermostat has a fan switch, because continuous fan operation is the only approved way to keep a faster blower motor within its temperature rating

questions.explanation: Power rises with roughly the cube of speed, so 1.10 cubed is about 1.33, meaning roughly 33 percent more power for 10 percent more speed, and a motor already at nameplate amps has no reserve for that. Belt stock, register adjustment, and a fan switch do not address the motor loading the change creates.

questions.question: What does a low-water cutoff protect a boiler against?

answers.text: High gas pressure at the manifold caused by a failed regulator that is delivering full inlet pressure directly to the burners
Frozen coils in the air handler
Excessive circulator speed
Firing or overheating when boiler water level falls too low, which can damage the boiler and create a hazard

questions.explanation: The low-water cutoff interrupts burner operation when water level is unsafe, preventing dry-firing damage and hazard, option D. Gas manifold pressure (A) is governed by the regulator and gas valve, frozen air-handler coils (B) concern a different system, and circulator speed (C) is set by the pump and its controls, not a water-level safety.

questions.question: A furnace starts its inducer on a call for heat, but the igniter never glows and the burners never light. The pressure switch contacts remain open, the vent is clear, and the inducer produces adequate vacuum. What does this pattern most strongly indicate?

answers.text: The pressure switch has failed and should be replaced after verifying adequate draft
The flame sensor is dirty and coated with oxide, so it is preventing the igniter from ever being energized
The gas valve is stuck open and flooding the heat exchanger
The high-limit switch is open because of low airflow

questions.explanation: The pressure switch proves draft before ignition is allowed, so adequate vacuum with contacts that stay open points to a failed switch, option A, once draft and tubing are verified. A dirty flame sensor (B) causes shutdown after light-off, not failure to start ignition, a stuck-open gas valve (C) would not hold off the igniter, and an open limit (D) does not explain the pressure-switch behavior.

questions.question: Supply ducts in a hot attic leak 15% of airflow. Which effect is most direct?

answers.text: Rooms receive more air than designed
Delivered capacity falls and run time and energy use rise
Static pressure in the rooms increases
Refrigerant charge automatically increases to compensate for the lost supply airflow

questions.explanation: Leaked supply air never reaches the rooms, so delivered capacity falls and the system runs longer using more energy, making B correct. A is opposite to the loss, room static does not rise from supply leakage, and duct leakage has no automatic effect on refrigerant charge.

questions.question: A communicating thermostat displays indoor temperature correctly but the outdoor unit never receives a cooling demand, while a conventional call wired at the air handler works. Where is the fault most likely isolated?

answers.text: Inside the compressor, because a compressor that cannot start also blocks demand signals from leaving the thermostat in communicating systems
In the refrigerant circuit, because low charge prevents the indoor board from acknowledging any demand regardless of the wiring between devices
Between the thermostat and the communicating indoor board
In the outdoor fan motor, because the fan must prove rotation before the system will pass a demand message from the thermostat indoors

questions.explanation: A working conventional call proves the equipment can run, and a correct temperature display proves the thermostat senses, so the break sits in the communication path to the indoor board. Compressor, charge, and fan conditions affect operation after a demand is received, not the delivery of the demand message itself.

questions.question: An EEV stepper's four coil windings are measured: three match the specified resistance and one reads open. The valve body moves freely in a known-good test. What is the correct repair?

answers.text: Replace the stepper motor/coil assembly or repair the harness fault, since the valve body itself has been shown to move freely
Replace the entire valve body and coil together in every case, because coil faults cannot be separated from the valve they drive on any design
Replace the outdoor control board, because an open coil winding is generated inside the board's driver chip rather than in the coil or its wiring
Add refrigerant until the valve opens further, because an open coil reading is a normal response to a system that is low on charge

questions.explanation: An open coil with a free valve body localizes the fault to the motor coil or its harness, which is serviced without discarding a sound valve body. Coil and body are separable on serviceable designs, the driver chip does not create an open winding in an external coil, and charge level has no relationship to a coil continuity reading.

questions.question: A furnace clocks at an input 20% above its rating plate after a gas-valve replacement. The most likely setup causes are:

answers.text: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed
A vent connector one size larger than the minimum, because a larger vent increases draft and pulls extra gas through the burner orifices
A sediment trap with a long capped leg, because the trap volume adds a reserve of gas that the meter counts as additional furnace input
A thermostat set several degrees above room temperature, because a larger temperature difference makes the gas valve deliver more fuel per hour

questions.explanation: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed. Vent size, trap volume, and thermostat setting do not change firing rate; excessive manifold pressure or oversized orifices do.

questions.question: A CO alarm sounds in a home with gas appliances and occupants report headaches that ease outdoors. What is the correct immediate response?

answers.text: Open one window near the alarm, reset it to silence the alert, and stay in the house to see whether it sounds again over the next several hours
Turn the thermostat up to burn off the carbon monoxide
Leave the building, get fresh air, and call emergency services or the gas utility before re-entering
Run the kitchen exhaust for an hour while staying inside to monitor

questions.explanation: Symptoms plus an alarm call for evacuation and professional response, not troubleshooting in place. Resetting the alarm while staying inside prolongs exposure. Heating does not remove CO, and relying on a kitchen fan while remaining indoors leaves occupants at risk if levels are high.

questions.question: A large refrigerant leak into a small, closed mechanical room is dangerous primarily because the vapor:

answers.text: Raises the room's oxygen concentration sharply
Displaces oxygen and can asphyxiate occupants
Turns instantly into a flammable liquid pool
Makes the room air strongly acidic on contact

questions.explanation: Refrigerant vapor is heavier than air and pools low, pushing oxygen out of the breathing zone, so ventilation and prompt evacuation protect occupants.

questions.question: An 80% furnace is replaced with a 96% condensing furnace reusing the old B-vent chimney path. What venting change is required?

answers.text: The B-vent can be kept unchanged because furnace vent categories are interchangeable whenever the vent diameter stays the same
The old vent can be kept if the installer raises the flue temperature by removing the new furnace's secondary heat exchanger
The new furnace needs its listed plastic or approved vent system; its cool, condensing exhaust cannot use the old B-vent as-is
The chimney should be capped and the new furnace vented into the attic space, where its exhaust is too cool to cause any harm

questions.explanation: Condensing furnaces produce cool, wet exhaust that requires listed corrosion-resistant venting routed outdoors. Vent categories are not interchangeable by diameter, removing a heat exchanger is not an installation option, and exhaust must never terminate in an attic.

questions.question: Case: A contractor collects a deposit, starts a change-out, then stops showing up and stops answering, with no justification offered. Which ground fits?

answers.text: Working outside the scope of a restricted license on one job
Obtaining a license by false or fraudulent representation
Abandoning or failing to perform, without justification, an HVACR contract or project
Knowingly allowing another licensee to work outside that licensee's scope of practice

questions.explanation: Abandoning or failing to perform, without justification, any HVACR contract or project is its own discipline ground. The absence of justification is part of the ground, not an afterthought.

georgia-hvac.quiz_title: Georgia HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: A walk-in system is started on a cold morning after sitting off all weekend. At startup the oil foams violently, oil pressure fluctuates, and a loud knocking is heard for several seconds. What event best explains this startup behavior?

answers.text: Refrigerant that migrated to the crankcase boiled off and liquid was drawn toward the cylinders
The discharge check valve opened too slowly, so hot gas backed up through the oil pump and aerated the oil from the top of the crankcase downward
The expansion valve opened fully at startup as designed, and the resulting normal superheat at the compressor caused the oil to foam in the sight glass
The condenser fans started before the compressor, lowering head pressure so much that the oil pump cavitated on cold, thick oil for the first minute

questions.explanation: During a long cold off period, refrigerant migrates to and condenses in the crankcase oil; at startup the pressure drop boils it off, foaming the oil and risking liquid slugging in the cylinders. A slow discharge check does not aerate oil through the pump, a normally feeding expansion valve maintains superheat rather than foaming oil, and early condenser fan operation does not cause crankcase migration or startup knocking.

questions.question: A homeowner asks why the new R-454B air handler runs its blower for a while after a leak sensor trips, even though cooling has stopped. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The blower is removing residual heat from the electric heat strips, a normal cool-down sequence that happens to coincide with the sensor alarm event
The blower pressurizes the duct system so refrigerant vapor is forced back through the leak point into the coil, resealing the system temporarily
The blower dilutes and disperses leaked refrigerant through the duct system so room concentration stays low
The blower run is a fault in itself, because mitigation design requires the air handler to shut down every moving part the instant a sensor trips

questions.explanation: Leak mitigation uses indoor airflow to dilute and disperse refrigerant so concentration in the occupied space stays low. The run is not a heat-strip cool-down, airflow cannot push vapor back into a leaking coil or reseal it, and the blower operation is an intended mitigation response rather than a second fault.

questions.question: Before handling the terminals of a run capacitor that was just removed from a running system, what must a technician do?

answers.text: Nothing, because capacitors discharge instantly when power is removed
Short the terminals together with an insulated screwdriver held in a bare hand as the standard method, as the preferred shop method
Discharge the capacitor safely (for example through a resistor) and verify with a meter that no charge remains
Reconnect it to the motor briefly so the motor windings drain the charge

questions.explanation: Capacitors can hold a dangerous charge after power is removed, so they must be discharged in a controlled way and verified with a meter before handling. Option A is false and is how technicians get shocked, while option B risks a violent arc and injury without a resistive discharge path. Option D is an uncontrolled method that can damage windings and still leave the charge state unknown.

questions.question: A modern residential gas furnace uses a hot-surface igniter. What material and behavior most accurately describe this igniter?

answers.text: A spark electrode that clicks continuously throughout the heating cycle to re-light the burners whenever the thermostat calls for heat
A silicon carbide or silicon nitride element that glows hot enough to ignite gas directly
A standing pilot that stays lit all season and lights the main burners
A thermocouple that generates voltage to open the gas valve

questions.explanation: The hot-surface igniter is a resistive silicon carbide or nitride element that glows to well above gas ignition temperature and lights the burners directly, which is option B. A spark electrode (A) describes direct-spark ignition, not hot-surface ignition, a standing pilot (C) describes older pilot systems, and a thermocouple (D) is a pilot safety sensor, not an igniter.

questions.question: A hydronic loop is filled with 50% propylene glycol where 30% would provide the needed freeze protection. Compared with water, the excess glycol will most likely:

answers.text: Lower heat output and raise pumping work, because excess glycol is more viscous and carries less heat per gallon, while adding unnecessary cost
Increase heat transfer and reduce circulator load
Have no effect on system performance at any concentration
Eliminate the need for corrosion inhibitors in the loop

questions.explanation: Glycol solutions transfer less heat and are more viscous than water, and the penalty grows with concentration, so over-concentrating derates coils and loads the circulator. Option B reverses both effects. Option C denies measured fluid properties that sizing must account for. Option D is wrong because glycol still requires maintained inhibitors, which degrade over time.

questions.question: An installer is sealing a medium-pressure supply trunk that runs through an unconditioned warehouse. Why does this duct warrant more rigorous sealing than a short low-pressure run inside the conditioned space?

answers.text: Higher-pressure duct is made of thinner metal, so the sealant is needed to hold the duct together structurally, with the mastic carrying the joint load and keeping the sections aligned under pressure in place of heavier fasteners or added reinforcement
Higher internal pressure drives more leakage through every unsealed seam, and air leaked outside the conditioned space is a total energy loss rather than a partial one
Sealing matters less at higher pressure because the pressure forces mastic into the gaps
Duct in unconditioned space only needs sealing at the registers, since trunk seams do not leak

questions.explanation: Leakage rises with the pressure pushing air out of the seams, and supply air lost into an unconditioned warehouse never reaches the rooms it was conditioned for. Option A is wrong because duct gauge generally gets heavier, not thinner, as pressure class rises, and sealant is never the structural fastener; option C is wrong because pressure pushes air out through gaps; it does not push sealant into them after the fact; option D is wrong because trunk seams are usually the largest leakage area on the system, well ahead of register boots.

questions.question: A wall-mounted carbon dioxide sensor for demand ventilation is installed directly in the supply-air discharge stream of a diffuser. What problem does this create?

answers.text: It over-reads carbon dioxide because supply air leaving the diffuser carries the highest carbon dioxide concentration found anywhere in the room
It will be damaged by carbon dioxide, which is corrosive to sensor elements at room levels
It has no effect, because concentration is identical at every point in the room at all times
It samples diluted supply air instead of room air, so it under-reads occupancy and the space gets under-ventilated

questions.explanation: Supply air is low in carbon dioxide and dilutes the sample, hiding the true room level from the controller. The error is an under-read, not an over-read. Room-level carbon dioxide does not corrode the sensor, and concentrations are not uniform while air is mixing.

questions.question: A furnace clocks at an input 20% above its rating plate after a gas-valve replacement. The most likely setup causes are:

answers.text: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed
A vent connector one size larger than the minimum, because a larger vent increases draft and pulls extra gas through the burner orifices
A sediment trap with a long capped leg, because the trap volume adds a reserve of gas that the meter counts as additional furnace input
A thermostat set several degrees above room temperature, because a larger temperature difference makes the gas valve deliver more fuel per hour

questions.explanation: Manifold pressure set too high or wrong-size orifices installed. Vent size, trap volume, and thermostat setting do not change firing rate; excessive manifold pressure or oversized orifices do.

questions.question: Why do traditional combustion air methods provide two openings, one high and one low, between a furnace room and the rest of the building or outdoors?

answers.text: Both openings are drains for condensate from the appliance
The high opening lets hot air and flue-related gases escape the enclosure while the low opening supplies cooler combustion air
The high opening is provided for cooling-season supply airflow and the low opening serves as the return-air path back to the air handler for the rest of the house
Two openings are required only so one can be blocked as a spare

questions.explanation: Warm air rises out the upper opening while denser supply air enters low, supporting both combustion supply and enclosure relief. Neither opening is a condensate drain. They are not the building's cooling or return-air system, and neither opening is intended to be blocked as a spare.

questions.question: A shop reviews a year of callbacks and finds most return visits trace to a handful of causes: missed drain problems, untested safeties, and rushed startups. What is the most valuable use of this analysis?

answers.text: Blame whichever technician has the most callbacks and change nothing else
Change the startup and quality-check process to attack those recurring causes, then track whether callback rates fall
Extend every equipment warranty silently for another full year so that callbacks cost the customer less paperwork and no one has to examine why the failures keep recurring
Stop recording callbacks so the rate appears to improve

questions.explanation: Callback analysis pays off when it drives process fixes for recurring root causes and the results are measured. Blame without process change repeats the failures, extending warranty terms does not reduce defects, and hiding data destroys the information needed to improve.

questions.question: A homeowner finished a 400-square-foot addition served by the existing system and now wants a changeout. What design step is required before selecting equipment?

answers.text: A new load calculation covering the enlarged conditioned space, rather than sizing from the original home alone
No calculation, because additions under 500 square feet are absorbed by the safety factor built into every residential system
Sizing by the addition's square footage at the same tons-per-square-foot ratio the original installer used decades ago
Selecting equipment one full ton larger than the old unit, which reliably covers any addition of this general size

questions.explanation: Added conditioned area changes the load and the room-by-room distribution, so a fresh calculation must include it. There is no automatic safety factor for additions, rules of thumb repeat old errors, and a flat one-ton bump is unrelated to the actual load.

questions.question: At a Georgia job's design friction rate, the duct chart values the designer is using for round branch ducts are: 6-inch = 110 cfm, 7-inch = 160 cfm, 8-inch = 230 cfm. A family room branch must deliver 185 cfm. Which size does the design select?

answers.text: 6-inch, because the smallest duct that produces high discharge velocity gives the room the best air mixing at the register
8-inch, because it is the smallest listed size whose chart capacity at the design friction rate meets the required 185 cfm
7-inch, because its chart capacity may be exceeded by up to twenty percent before the next size is required by the method
10-inch, because branch ducts are routinely selected two sizes above the calculated need to leave room for future additions

questions.explanation: B is correct: at the design friction rate the 7-inch duct carries only 160 cfm, short of the 185 cfm the room requires, so the design moves to the 8-inch size at 230 cfm, the smallest listed size that meets the requirement. A selects a duct carrying barely half the required airflow. C invents an over-capacity allowance that would leave the room under-aired and unbalance the system. D oversizes far beyond the chart selection with no design basis.

questions.question: Why must a refrigerant distributor create a deliberate pressure drop at its nozzle?

answers.text: So the liquid refrigerant is completely flashed to vapor before it enters the circuits, because evaporator circuits are designed to be fed with dry vapor only
So the expansion valve can be eliminated from the system, because the distributor nozzle alone is intended to meter the entire refrigerant flow to the coil
So the pressure in the evaporator is raised above suction pressure, because a distributor works by pressurizing the coil rather than by dividing the flow
So the two-phase mixture distributes evenly to every circuit despite small differences in circuit pressure drop

questions.explanation: The nozzle pressure drop dominates small circuit-to-circuit differences, forcing an even split of the mixed liquid and flash gas to each circuit. The distributor must feed a liquid-vapor mixture, not dry vapor, the TXV still does the metering ahead of the distributor, and the distributor divides flow at a pressure loss rather than pressurizing the coil.

questions.question: A homeowner asks why the new R-454B air handler runs its blower for a while after a leak sensor trips, even though cooling has stopped. What is the correct explanation?

answers.text: The blower is removing residual heat from the electric heat strips, a normal cool-down sequence that happens to coincide with the sensor alarm event
The blower pressurizes the duct system so refrigerant vapor is forced back through the leak point into the coil, resealing the system temporarily
The blower dilutes and disperses leaked refrigerant through the duct system so room concentration stays low
The blower run is a fault in itself, because mitigation design requires the air handler to shut down every moving part the instant a sensor trips

questions.explanation: Leak mitigation uses indoor airflow to dilute and disperse refrigerant so concentration in the occupied space stays low. The run is not a heat-strip cool-down, airflow cannot push vapor back into a leaking coil or reseal it, and the blower operation is an intended mitigation response rather than a second fault.

questions.question: On a fixed-orifice system being checked with a manufacturer's target-superheat chart, a technician records the outdoor dry-bulb temperature. What second temperature does the chart require as its other input?

answers.text: Liquid-line temperature at the condenser outlet
Indoor wet-bulb temperature, which reflects the total indoor heat and moisture load
Suction-line temperature at the compressor inlet
Return-air dry-bulb temperature only, with no moisture measurement, measured at the return-air grille

questions.explanation: Target-superheat charts are entered with outdoor dry bulb and indoor wet bulb, because wet bulb captures both the sensible and latent load on the evaporator. Option A is a measurement used for subcooling, not a chart input, and option C is the value used to compute actual superheat, not to look up the target. Option D omits the moisture component, which is exactly what wet bulb adds to the calculation.

questions.question: In a zone-valve hydronic system, how is heat delivered to only the zone that is calling?

answers.text: One circulator per zone runs while all zone valves stay open, and each zone is heated in turn by timers in the boiler control rather than by its own thermostat
A single boiler pump reverses direction for each zone
Each zone has a motorized valve opened by its own thermostat, while a shared circulator moves water through whichever valves are open
Each zone has its own boiler controlled by one thermostat

questions.explanation: Zone-valve zoning uses one circulator and a valve per zone; a calling thermostat opens its valve and the end switch or control starts the circulator. Option A describes circulator zoning, the alternative arrangement. Option B is wrong because circulators do not reverse to select zones. Option D multiplies boilers instead of zoning one boiler's output.

questions.question: A homeowner calls because the outdoor unit is steaming, the outdoor fan has stopped, and a whoosh was heard, while the unit is heating on a frosty morning. What should the technician explain first?

answers.text: The compressor has failed and the unit should be shut off at the breaker immediately
The refrigerant charge is escaping as steam and the area should be evacuated
This is a normal defrost: the reversing valve shifted, the fan stopped, frost is melting into visible vapor, and the cycle will end and heating will resume in a few minutes
The unit has mistakenly switched to cooling for the rest of the day

questions.explanation: Steam-like vapor, a stopped outdoor fan, and the reversing-valve whoosh are the classic signs of a normal defrost melting accumulated frost. Option A declares a failure without any fault evidence, option B mistakes water vapor for refrigerant, which is not visible as steam in this way, and option D overstates a minutes-long defrost as a day-long mode change.

questions.question: An electronic bypass arrangement uses a plenum static pressure sensor wired to the control. What does the control do with that signal?

answers.text: It uses the signal only to log pressure for a service report, because electronic bypass dampers are positioned by zone thermostat count and never by measured duct pressure
It converts the pressure signal into a call for second-stage heat, because high plenum pressure is the panel's standard indication that more capacity is needed in the zones
It modulates the bypass damper to hold the set static pressure
It shuts the bypass damper tighter as pressure rises, because relieving a zoned system requires forcing all blower airflow through whichever zones remain open

questions.explanation: In an electronic bypass system the sensor reports plenum static pressure and the control drives the modulating bypass damper to hold the chosen setpoint. The signal is a working control input rather than a log entry, high pressure calls for relief rather than more capacity, and closing the bypass further would raise pressure instead of relieving it.

questions.question: On a ladder diagram, a thermostat contact, a limit switch, and a relay coil appear in series on one rung, and the relay contacts are on another rung. If the limit opens, what happens?

answers.text: Only the thermostat is bypassed and the relay stays energized
The relay coil de-energizes and its contacts return to their shelf state
The relay contacts weld closed to maintain operation
Power flows backward through the coil to the transformer

questions.explanation: Series devices all control the same coil, so an open limit breaks the circuit and de-energizes the relay. Nothing is bypassed by an opening switch. Contacts do not weld as a normal response to losing coil power, and current does not flow backward to sustain the rung.

questions.question: Windows condense heavily on cold winter mornings in a tight new home with a large family, showers, and cooking. Indoor humidity reads 48%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: The humidifier is undersized, so raising indoor humidity further will warm the window glass and stop the condensation from forming
The windows are leaking refrigerant, because condensation on glass is a recognized sign of a cooling-system charge problem in winter
The furnace is oversized for cooling, which explains winter window moisture even though the cooling system is not operating at all
Indoor moisture generation exceeds removal, so humidity must be lowered and ventilation or exhaust increased rather than adding humidification.

questions.explanation: Condensation means indoor dew point exceeds the cold glass temperature; the fix is less indoor moisture and more removal through ventilation and exhaust. Adding humidity makes it worse, windows contain no refrigerant, and cooling sizing is irrelevant to a winter moisture balance.

questions.question: Supply ducts run through an unconditioned ventilated attic in a hot climate. Why is duct insulation with a sealed vapor retarder required there?

answers.text: It makes the duct airtight, so joints in attic ducts never need to be sealed with mastic or approved tape at installation
It limits heat gain into the cold airstream and keeps the duct surface from sweating.
It raises supply-air temperature in summer so registers feel warmer and occupants stop reporting cold drafts in the morning
It replaces structural duct support, allowing long attic runs to rest directly on ceiling joists without hangers or straps

questions.explanation: Insulation slows heat gain and the outer vapor retarder stops moist attic air from condensing on cold metal. Insulation does not seal joints, warming supply air defeats cooling, and insulation provides no structural support.

questions.question: Why does the furnace or air handler blower matter to a cooling system's rated combination?

answers.text: The blower matters only for heating season, because cooling capacity is set entirely at the outdoor unit and airflow is secondary
Blower airflow across the coil is part of the tested combination, and wrong airflow changes capacity, efficiency, and dehumidification
A stronger blower always raises the rating, so oversizing the air handler is a reliable way to gain extra efficiency points
Blower selection affects only noise level, since the coil removes the same moisture regardless of the air volume crossing it

questions.explanation: Rated performance assumes a specified airflow; too much or too little distorts sensible and latent capacity. The blower is central in cooling as well as heating, more airflow is not automatically better, and moisture removal is strongly airflow-dependent.

questions.question: A contractor is hired to install a comfort-heating system for an office building that uses low-pressure steam with piping, ducts, and related mechanical equipment. Which heating license group covers this work?

answers.text: Heating Group 1, because the system uses steam or hot water for comfort heating in a building.
Heating Group 3, because any direct comfort-heating system in a commercial building falls in that group.
Heating Group 2, because the system circulates conditioned air and serves a nonresidential building.
No heating group, because steam comfort heating is treated as plumbing work rather than heating work.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Heating Group 1 is the heating system of a building using high or low pressure steam, vapor, or hot water, including appurtenant piping, ducts, and equipment, for comfort heating. B is wrong because Group 3 covers direct systems using electric elements or combustion heat exchange, not steam systems. C is wrong because Group 2 requires an integral refrigeration system over 15 tons circulating air. D is wrong because this steam system is expressly a heating group, Group 1.

questions.question: An installer proposes running plastic gas pipe above ground along a North Carolina building wall and then indoors to a furnace, arguing plastic is approved gas piping without location limits. Which correction is right?

answers.text: Plastic pipe may be used indoors if it is painted, because paint supplies the protection the location rules are seeking

Plastic fuel-gas piping is permitted only underground outdoors, must be installed with an electrically conductive tracer wire, and must transition to above-ground or indoor piping only through approved risers and fittings
Plastic pipe may be used anywhere steel is used, because the two materials carry identical location permissions in the code
Plastic pipe is prohibited for fuel gas in all locations, including underground service lines buried outside the building

questions.explanation: B is correct: plastic pipe for fuel gas is limited to underground use outdoors, must be buried with a tracer wire (minimum 18 AWG, insulation suitable for direct burial) so the line can be located, and may come above ground only through an approved anodeless riser or transition fitting. A is wrong because painting does not make above-ground or indoor plastic gas piping permissible. C is wrong because plastic carries location limits that steel does not. D is wrong because underground outdoor plastic piping is an approved and common application.

florida-hvac.quiz_title: Florida HVAC Exam Prep FREE Sample Exam — Fixed Set

questions.question: Three compressors run in parallel on a rack. One compressor keeps losing oil while the others gain oil, and there is no external leak. What part of the oil management system should be checked first?

answers.text: The liquid-line filter driers, because a restricted drier core is the component that normally meters oil from the reservoir into each individual crankcase
The oil level regulators and the oil reservoir supply feeding each crankcase
The thermostatic expansion valves, because each valve is responsible for returning a measured share of the system oil directly to its own compressor
The condenser fan cycling control, because uneven condenser airflow is what distributes oil unequally among compressors piped in parallel on a rack

questions.explanation: On parallel racks, individual oil level regulators fed from a common reservoir control each crankcase level, so a sticking regulator or low reservoir supply starves one machine. Liquid driers clean refrigerant and do not meter oil to crankcases, expansion valves meter refrigerant to evaporators rather than oil to compressors, and condenser fan control affects head pressure, not per-compressor oil distribution.

questions.question: A TXV system runs with a sweating, frost-covered suction line to the compressor. Readings: suction 156 psig, superheat 2°F, subcooling 6°F, compressor amps 112% of rated, discharge superheat low, airflow and charge weight both verified correct, and the frost persists after the bulb is re-secured and insulated. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: A dirty condenser coil restricting heat rejection, which raises head pressure sharply while leaving evaporator superheat near its setpoint
A restricted liquid-line drier, which would starve the valve, raise superheat, and show a temperature drop across the drier body
A TXV stuck open
A low refrigerant charge, which starves the evaporator and produces high superheat with low suction pressure, the reverse of this pattern

questions.explanation: Near-zero superheat with high suction pressure and frost reaching the compressor is liquid floodback from a valve feeding far beyond the load, confirmed when re-securing the bulb changes nothing. A low charge and a drier restriction both starve the evaporator and raise superheat, and a dirty condenser attacks the high side while the TXV still holds superheat.

questions.question: An inspection finds heavy flaking rust and scale shedding from inside the heat exchanger onto the burners below. What is the best interpretation?

answers.text: The condition is normal for any exchanger over five years old and requires no documentation, cleaning, or follow-up of any kind
The scale proves the exchanger is made of stainless steel, because only stainless surfaces produce visible flaking as they age
Advanced corrosion weakening the exchanger
The deposits prove the furnace has been underfired for years, because only low temperatures allow any corrosion products to form

questions.explanation: Heavy flaking and shedding indicate advanced corrosion that thins and weakens exchanger metal and can progress to holes and flue-gas leakage. Option A dismisses a documented deterioration finding, option B reverses the material evidence, and option D misattributes corrosion that is commonly driven by condensate and temperature conditions, not simple underfiring.

questions.question: An oil burner consistently ignites with a loud puff several seconds after the motor starts, then runs cleanly. Spark is strong and present on time. The delay most likely comes from:

answers.text: A cad cell with low resistance in darkness, caused by a cracked cell housing that admits room light into the burner compartment even when the access panel is closed and the flame is completely out
Slow oil delivery to the nozzle — for example air in the line, a clogged nozzle strainer, or a weak delayed-opening solenoid — so fuel arrives after the trial has begun
Excessive stack draft pulling the flame off the head
A thermostat calling on both W1 and W2 together

questions.explanation: If ignition energy is on time but fuel arrives late, oil sprays into a hot chamber and lights with a puff when it finally reaches the arc. Option A would make the control think flame exists before startup and cause a different lockout fault. Option C destabilizes an established flame rather than delaying fuel. Option D is a gas-furnace staging concept that does not apply to this oil burner sequence.

questions.question: A homeowner expects zoning dampers to cure weak airflow that exists today with all rooms calling, on an undersized common trunk. Why will zoning alone disappoint?

answers.text: Zoning increases the capacity of the common trunk, so weak airflow with all zones calling proves the trunk is oversized rather than undersized for the equipment
Dampers add resistance and only redistribute air; they do not enlarge a trunk that is already too small for total airflow
Weak airflow with all zones calling is caused by the zone panel withholding blower speed, and removing the panel restores full trunk capacity without any duct change at all
Zoning cures total airflow problems whenever one room is weak, because closing other branches permanently is an accepted substitute for sizing the common duct to the equipment

questions.explanation: Dampers redistribute the air the blower delivers and add resistance of their own, so they cannot cure a common trunk that is already too small when every zone calls together. Zoning can send a larger share to one area by restricting others, but total airflow capacity still depends on the trunk, the blower, and total static pressure.

questions.question: Comfort complaint. A system satisfies its thermostat in about seven minutes and shuts off while far bedrooms remain 4 degrees warm. The thermostat sits on a wall directly in the discharge path of a nearby supply register, and a thermometer held at the thermostat reads several degrees cooler than a thermometer in the room center while the system runs. Between cycles the two readings converge. What is the most likely cause?

answers.text: An oversized air conditioner short-cycling on capacity, which would satisfy the whole house's sensible load quickly and would not leave the thermostat reading colder than the room only while air is moving
A thermostat with a drifting sensor reading low, which would read off from room temperature at all times, including between cycles when these two readings converge
Supply air washing over the thermostat and satisfying it early
A weak compressor losing capacity mid-cycle, which would lengthen rather than shorten run times and would warm the supply air instead of cooling the thermostat's wall

questions.explanation: Discharge air blows straight onto the thermostat, cooling its sensor below true room temperature while the system runs, so it satisfies in minutes while distant rooms stay warm; between cycles the sensor recovers and readings converge. Oversizing satisfies the whole space, not just the thermostat wall, a drifting sensor would disagree with room temperature at rest too, and a weak compressor extends run time instead of cutting it to seven minutes.

questions.question: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) is used for part of a home's gas distribution. Besides following the manufacturer's instructions for fittings and support, what widely required safety measure applies to the CSST system?

answers.text: Electrical bonding of the gas piping system to reduce lightning-related damage risk
Painting the tubing black so it looks like iron pipe
Burying it without any protective sleeve or coating wherever it passes through concrete, masonry, or underground soil
